results.summary: This analog block implements a very slow ring oscillator whose output is brought out on two analog pins. It is used by powering the board at 1.8 V and observing the signal on analog pins 0 and 1. The documentation is extremely thin, giving only a one-line description and no schematic, frequency measurement, or test results, so the exact topology and performance are unclear. The design is notable for its extremely low oscillation frequency and its use of the analog I/O pins.

This project is a tiny FPGA fabric that can be programmed using Yosys and nextpnr. It is designed to be compatible with the Tiny Tapeout interface, allowing simple designs to be mapped directly onto the fabric. The fabric is implemented as an ASIC and is intended for educational use. The exact architecture and configuration details are not fully described in the documentation.

This project is a combinational 7-segment decoder that converts a BCD nibble into the standard gfedcba pattern for a seven-segment display. It is designed for educational purposes and can be used to drive a seven-segment display. The design is purely combinational and does not require any clock. The output is directly observable on the seven-segment display pins.

This project implements a comparator and a finite state machine. The comparator compares two input values and produces an output indicating their relationship. The FSM controls the operation of the comparator. The design is implemented using sequential logic and logic gates. The exact functionality and use cases are not fully detailed in the documentation.

FinSec-1 is a hardware-only AS-68M fingerprint verification ASIC that implements the complete UART command protocol as a 14-state deterministic finite state machine, with no microcontroller or CPU in the trusted path. It is designed for security applications and uses a UART interface for communication. The design is implemented as an ASIC and includes a sensor interface. The exact fingerprint verification algorithm is not described in the documentation.

This project is a demoscene implementation of Conway's Game of Life intended to display on a VGA board. The documentation states only that it shows the Game of Life on the VGA board, with no details on resolution, timing, or control interface. The design uses a VGA PMOD that provides the VGA connector and resistor-ladder DAC. The output is a video signal that can be observed on a VGA monitor.
